The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

For $b>0$, let $\mu_b$ be the probability measure on $\mathbb R$ supported on $(0,+\infty)$ with Lebesgue density $x\mapsto b^{-1}e^{-x/b}$ there and zero elsewhere. For every Borel set $A\subseteq\mathbb R$, define

$$
\operatorname{Lap}(b)(A)=\frac12\mu_b(A\cap(0,+\infty))+\frac12\mu_b(\{x>0:-x\in A\}).
$$

Thus $\operatorname{Lap}(b)$ is the equal mixture of the positive exponential law and its reflection in the origin. Define $\operatorname{Lap}(0)$ to be the point mass at $0$.

Assume Countable Choice. For $\lambda>0$, the density
$$f_\lambda(t)=\begin{cases}\lambda e^{-\lambda t},&t>0,\\0,&t\le0\end{cases}$$
defines a probability law on $\mathbb R$ with survival
$S(t)=e^{-\lambda t}$ for $t\ge0$. For $k,\eta>0$, the density
$$f_{k,\eta}(t)=\begin{cases}\dfrac{k}{\eta}(t/\eta)^{k-1}e^{-(t/\eta)^k},&t>0,\\0,&t\le0\end{cases}$$
defines a probability law with survival $S(t)=e^{-(t/\eta)^k}$ for $t\ge0$.
Each law is unique among probability laws on $[0,\infty)$ with that survival.
The density hazards are respectively $\lambda$ and
$\dfrac{k}{\eta}(t/\eta)^{k-1}$ for $t>0$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$U,V \subseteq \mathbb R^n$ be open and let $T : U \to V$ be a
$C^1$ diffeomorphism. For every nonnegative Lebesgue measurable
$f : V \to [0,\infty]$,
$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]), and let $a_i \le b_i$ be reals for $i<n$. Write

$$R^{\circ} := \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i < x_i < b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}, \qquad \overline{R} := [a,b] = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i \le x_i \le b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}$$

([[def-multidimensional-rectangle-and-volume]]). Then $R^{\circ}$ is open and
$\overline{R}$ is closed, so both are Borel and Lebesgue measurable, and **every**
set $R$ with $R^{\circ} \subseteq R \subseteq \overline{R}$ is Lebesgue
measurable with

$$\lambda_n(R) \;=\; \prod_{i<n}(b_i-a_i).$$

In particular this covers the four one-dimensional face conventions in each
coordinate — the open box, the closed box $[a,b]$, the half-open box
$B(a,b) = \prod_{i<n}(a_i,b_i]$ of [[def-half-open-box]], and every mixture of
them, in any combination of coordinates — and it gives measure $0$ to all of them
whenever $a_i = b_i$ for some $i<n$. For a half-open box with infinite
parameters the value is already
$\lambda_n(B) = \operatorname{vol}(B)$ ([[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]]).

derivations.claim: Put $A_+=A\cap(0,+\infty)$ and $A_-=A\cap(-\infty,0)$. By [F1] and [F2], the positive mixture half contributes $\frac12\int_{A_+}b^{-1}e^{-x/b}\,d\lambda(x)$. Applying [F3] to reflection $T(x)=-x$ and $y\mapsto\mathbf1_{A_-}(y)b^{-1}e^{y/b}$ shows that the reflected half contributes $\frac12\int_{A_-}b^{-1}e^{y/b}\,d\lambda(y)$. On $A_+$, $e^{-x/b}=e^{-|x|/b}$; on $A_-$, $e^{y/b}=e^{-|y|/b}$. The singleton at zero has Lebesgue measure zero by [F4]. Hence $\operatorname{Lap}(b)(A)=\int_A(2b)^{-1}e^{-|z|/b}\,d\lambda(z)$.

The identity in step 1.1 holds for every Borel set $A$. Its integrand is nonnegative and measurable; thus every Lebesgue-null Borel set has zero $\operatorname{Lap}(b)$ measure, and the displayed function is the claimed Radon–Nikodym density.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

For every $b>0$, the probability measure $\operatorname{Lap}(b)$ is absolutely continuous with respect to Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb R$ and has density

$$
z\longmapsto \frac{1}{2b}e^{-|z|/b}.
$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B)$ be measurable spaces. Their
**product sigma-algebra** is

$$\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B := \sigma(\{A \times B : A \in \mathcal A,\ B \in \mathcal B\}),$$

the sigma-algebra on $X \times Y$ generated by the measurable rectangles of
[[def-measurable-rectangle]].

For the empty family, put $\prod_{i<0}X_i:=\{()\}$ and define its **empty
product sigma-algebra** by

$$\bigotimes_{i<0}\mathcal A_i:=\{\varnothing,\{()\}\}.$$

For a nonempty finite family of measurable spaces $(X_i,\mathcal A_i)$ with
$i<n$, the **finite product sigma-algebra** is defined recursively by

$$\bigotimes_{i<1}\mathcal A_i := \mathcal A_0,\qquad \bigotimes_{i<n+1}\mathcal A_i := \left(\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathcal A_i\right)\otimes\mathcal A_n.$$

This recursive definition is the finite base case used later when the library
passes to countable product constructions.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces. Then:

1. the set function $E \mapsto (\mu \times \nu)(E)$ of
   [[def-product-measure-on-sigma-finite-spaces]] is a measure on
   $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$;
2. for measurable rectangles,
   $$(\mu \times \nu)(A \times B)=\mu(A)\nu(B),$$
   with the nonnegative extended-product convention $0\cdot\infty=\infty\cdot0=0$;
3. the measure $\mu \times \nu$ is sigma-finite; and
4. it is the unique measure on $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$ with the
   rectangle formula.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and define
$$\nu_f(A):=\int_A f\,d\mu \qquad (A\in\mathcal A).$$
Then $\nu_f$ is a measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$.

Let $\mathcal P$ be a pi-system on $X$ generating $\mathcal A$, and let $\mu,\nu$ be measures on $(X,\mathcal A)$ that agree on $\mathcal P$. Suppose there is an increasing sequence $(P_n)$ in $\mathcal P$ with

$$X=\bigcup_nP_n,\qquad \mu(P_n)=\nu(P_n)<+\infty\quad(n\in\mathbb N).$$

Then $\mu=\nu$ on $\mathcal A$.

Let $X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ be random elements on a
common probability space. For each $i$, write

$$\sigma(X_i):=\{X_i^{-1}(B):B\in\Sigma_i\}\subseteq\mathcal F.$$

The family $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ is **independent** when the sigma-algebras
$(\sigma(X_i))_{i\in I}$ are independent in the sense of
[[def-independent-sigma-algebras-and-events]].

When $\Sigma_i$ is a Borel sigma-algebra, this agrees with the notation
$\sigma(X_i)$ from [[def-sigma-algebra-generated-by-a-function]].

For all real $x,y$,
$$\exp(x+y)=\exp(x)\exp(y).$$

derivations.claim: Define $f(z)=\prod_{i=1}^d f_b(z_i)=(2b)^{-d}\exp(-\|z\|_1/b)$; the equality factoring the exponential of a finite sum uses [F8]. The function is nonnegative and product-measurable. Repeated application of [F4] gives $\int_{\mathbb R^d} f(z)\,d\lambda^d(z)=\prod_{i=1}^d\int_{\mathbb R}f_b(x)\,d\lambda(x)=1$, using [F1] for each one-dimensional integral. By [F5], $\nu(A)=\int_A f\,d\lambda^d$ is therefore a probability measure.

For a measurable rectangle $A=\prod_{i=1}^d A_i$, repeated Tonelli integration [F4] gives $\nu(A)=\prod_{i=1}^d\int_{A_i}f_b\,d\lambda=\prod_{i=1}^d\operatorname{Lap}(b)(A_i)$. The finite product law has this same rectangle value by [F3]. Rectangles form a generating pi-system by [F2]; both measures are finite, hence sigma-finite, so [F6] identifies $\nu$ with $\operatorname{Lap}(b)^{\otimes d}$ on the entire product sigma-algebra. The rectangular product law also gives independence of the coordinate projections and their stated marginals by [F7].

Let $U$ be a nonempty set of possible records and let $\mathbb N_0=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$. A database is a function $D:U\to\mathbb N_0$ with finite support $\operatorname{supp}(D)=\{u\in U:D(u)\ne0\}$; $D(u)$ is the number of occurrences of record $u$. Let $\mathcal D$ be the set of databases and equip it with the power-set sigma-algebra. For $u\in U$, let $\mathbf 1_{\{u\}}$ be the function that is one at $u$ and zero elsewhere. Two databases $D,D'\in\mathcal D$ are neighbors, written $D\sim D'$, when $D'=D+\mathbf 1_{\{u\}}$ or $D=D'+\mathbf 1_{\{u\}}$ for some $u\in U$.

A randomized mechanism with output measurable space $(Y,\mathcal B)$ is a probability kernel $K$ from $\mathcal D$ to $Y$: for each $D\in\mathcal D$, $A\mapsto K(D,A)$ is a probability measure on $(Y,\mathcal B)$, and for each $A\in\mathcal B$, $D\mapsto K(D,A)$ is measurable. Given $\varepsilon\ge0$ and $0\le\delta\le1$, the mechanism is $(\varepsilon,\delta)$-differentially private if, for every ordered neighboring pair $D\sim D'$ and every output event $A\in\mathcal B$,

$$
K(D,A)\le e^{\varepsilon}K(D',A)+\delta.
$$

The mechanism is $\varepsilon$-differentially private, or pure $\varepsilon$-differentially private, when $\delta=0$. The ordered-pair quantifier includes both directions because $\sim$ is symmetric.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $d\ge1$ and let $f:\mathcal D\to\mathbb R^d$ be a query on databases with the add/remove adjacency relation. Write $\|x\|_1=\sum_{j=1}^d|x_j|$. When the set of adjacent-pair differences has an attained finite maximum, the global $L^1$ sensitivity of $f$ is

$$
\Delta_1 f=\max_{D\sim D'}\|f(D)-f(D')\|_1.
$$

The sensitivity is finite when this maximum is finite.

For $b>0$, let $\mu_b$ be the probability measure on $\mathbb R$ supported on $(0,+\infty)$ with Lebesgue density $x\mapsto b^{-1}e^{-x/b}$ there and zero elsewhere. For every Borel set $A\subseteq\mathbb R$, define

$$
\operatorname{Lap}(b)(A)=\frac12\mu_b(A\cap(0,+\infty))+\frac12\mu_b(\{x>0:-x\in A\}).
$$

Thus $\operatorname{Lap}(b)$ is the equal mixture of the positive exponential law and its reflection in the origin. Define $\operatorname{Lap}(0)$ to be the point mass at $0$.

Let $(S,\Sigma)$ and $(T_i,\Tau_i)$ for $i<n$ be measurable spaces, with
$n<\infty$, and let $K_i:S\to T_i$ be probability kernels with the same
source. There is a unique probability kernel
$$K:S\to\prod_{i<n}T_i$$
whose evaluation on every measurable rectangle is
$$K(s,\prod_{i<n}B_i)=\prod_{i<n}K_i(s,B_i).$$
For $n=0$, the target is the empty-product singleton and $K$ is its point
mass. For $n>0$, the product sigma-algebra is the recursive finite product
sigma-algebra.

Let $(X,\mathcal T)$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]). The
**Borel sigma-algebra of $X$** is the sigma-algebra generated by its open sets:

$$\mathcal B(X):=\sigma_X(\mathcal T).$$

Its members are the **Borel subsets** of $X$. The generated sigma-algebra exists
and is minimal by [[thm-generated-sigma-algebra-exists-and-is-minimal]].

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $n,m\ge1$. Every continuous map
$f : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^m$ is Borel measurable in
the sense of [[def-borel-and-lebesgue-measurable-function-on-rn]].

A **measure kernel** from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$ is a map $K:S\times\Tau\to[0,\infty]$ such that, for every $s\in S$, $A\mapsto K(s,A)$ is a measure on $(T,\Tau)$, and for every $A\in\Tau$, $s\mapsto K(s,A)$ is $\Sigma$-measurable. Measures and measurability have the meanings in [[def-measure]] and [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]; the evaluation functions use the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,\infty]$.

A **probability kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)=1$ for every s. A **finite kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)<\infty$ for every s; there need not be a common bound on these masses. A **uniformly sigma-finite kernel**, in the convention of this page, comes with a specified sequence $T_n\in\Tau$ increasing to T such that $K(s,T_n)<\infty$ for every s and n. This is a common measurable exhaustion, not a bound uniform in s. A finite kernel has the constant exhaustion $T_n=T$. An arbitrary measure kernel is not assumed to have such an exhaustion.

All these requirements are pointwise in s, not merely almost everywhere for an unspecified measure on S. If T is empty, its only measure is zero, so a probability kernel into T can exist only when S is empty. If S is empty, the kernel requirements are vacuous. The zero kernel is finite. This definition selects no versions and uses no choice axiom.

derivations.claim: By [F2], $\Delta_1 f$ is finite and nonnegative, so the zero and positive branches cover every allowed input; if $\Delta_1 f>0$, the scale $b=\Delta_1 f/\varepsilon$ is positive. By [A1], [F3], and [F4], the noise vector has a probability law $\nu=\operatorname{Lap}(b)^{\otimes d}$. For each database $D$, define the output law as the pushforward of $\nu$ under $z\mapsto f(D)+z$; the inverse translation is continuous, so [F7] makes the preimage of every Borel set Borel and this is a probability measure.

If $\Delta_1 f=0$, assign the point mass at $f(D)$, which is a probability measure on the Borel output space. For either branch and each Borel event $A$, the evaluation $D\mapsto K(D,A)$ is measurable because every subset of the database domain is measurable by [F1]. Thus the assignment is a probability kernel as required by [F6].

Let $\mathcal D$ be the finite-support count functions on a nonempty record universe, with add/remove-one-occurrence adjacency. Let $R$ be a nonempty finite set independent of the database, and let $u:\mathcal D\times R\to\mathbb R$ be a real-valued utility. When the set of adjacent-pair utility differences has an attained finite maximum, the global utility sensitivity of $u$ is
$$
\Delta_u=\max_{D\sim D',\,r\in R}|u(D,r)-u(D',r)|.
$$
The sensitivity is positive when $\Delta_u>0$; the exponential mechanism on this page uses that positive-sensitivity case.

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in [[lem-exponential-series-has-infinite-radius]]. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image ([[def-canonical-natural]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]), and powers and series are those of [[def-integer-power]] and [[def-series]].

This is a real power series centred at $0$ ([[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]]). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.

A **probability measure** on a measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a measure $\mathbb P$ with $\mathbb P(X)=1$ ([[def-measure]]). The triple $(X,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ is a **probability space** ([[def-measure-space]]); $X$ is its sample space and the members of $\mathcal A$ are its events.

Let $U$ be a nonempty set of possible records and let $\mathbb N_0=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$. A database is a function $D:U\to\mathbb N_0$ with finite support $\operatorname{supp}(D)=\{u\in U:D(u)\ne0\}$; $D(u)$ is the number of occurrences of record $u$. The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

A measurable space $(E,\mathcal E)$ is **standard Borel** if there are a Polish space $P$ and a bijection $h:E\to P$ such that $A\in\mathcal E$ exactly when $h[A]$ is Borel in $P$. Thus the measurable structure is part of the datum; no particular compatible Polish topology on $E$ is selected.

A **measure kernel** from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$ is a map $K:S\times\Tau\to[0,\infty]$ such that, for every $s\in S$, $A\mapsto K(s,A)$ is a measure on $(T,\Tau)$, and for every $A\in\Tau$, $s\mapsto K(s,A)$ is $\Sigma$-measurable. Measures and measurability have the meanings in [[def-measure]] and [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]; the evaluation functions use the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,\infty]$.

A **probability kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)=1$ for every s. A **finite kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)<\infty$ for every s; there need not be a common bound on these masses. A **uniformly sigma-finite kernel**, in the convention of this page, comes with a specified sequence $T_n\in\Tau$ increasing to T such that $K(s,T_n)<\infty$ for every s and n. This is a common measurable exhaustion, not a bound uniform in s. A finite kernel has the constant exhaustion $T_n=T$. An arbitrary measure kernel is not assumed to have such an exhaustion.

All these requirements are pointwise in s, not merely almost everywhere for an unspecified measure on S. If T is empty, its only measure is zero, so a probability kernel into T can exist only when S is empty. If S is empty, the kernel requirements are vacuous. The zero kernel is finite. This definition selects no versions and uses no choice axiom.

Assume AC. Let $(E,\mathcal E)$ and $(F,\mathcal F)$ be standard Borel spaces, let $\lambda$ be a probability measure on $E$, and let $M$ and $R$ be probability kernels from $E$ to $F$. Then there is an $(\mathcal E\otimes\mathcal F)$-measurable function $r:E\times F\to[0,\infty]$ such that, for $\lambda$-almost every $x$ and every $B\in\mathcal F$,
$$M(x,B)=\int_B r(x,y)\,R(x,dy).$$

Approximate each of the first $N$ sets closely enough that their finite union has arbitrarily small symmetric-difference measure from $U_N$. Thus $\mathcal E_\rho$ is a sigma-algebra containing $\mathcal C$, so it is the full target sigma-algebra. For any measurable $B$, choose $C_n\in\mathcal C$ with $\rho(B\mathbin\triangle C_n)\to0$. Then both $K(h,C_n)\to K(h,B)$ and $L(h,C_n)\to L(h,B)$, so the two inequalities on $\mathcal C$ pass to every measurable $B$.

Write $a=\exp(\varepsilon)\ge1$ and $c=\exp(-\varepsilon)=1/a>0$ by [F9]. On $G$, set $p_0=\min\{\max\{p,cq\},aq\}$, $\alpha=\int(p-aq)_+\,dM$, and $\beta=\int(cq-p)_+\,dM$. These quantities are finite and measurable in $h$ by [F5] and [F8]. The sets $A_h=\{y:p(h,y)>aq(h,y)\}$ and $B_h=\{y:p(h,y)<cq(h,y)\}$ are measurable by [F7]. Hence $\max\{\alpha,\beta\}\le\delta$.

Its denominator is positive and $0\le t_+\le1$ because $a\ge1$, so $p_0\le r\le aq$ and $\int r\,dM=m+t_+(a-m)=1$. If $m>1$, let $t_-=(m-1)/(m-c)$ and $r=p_0-t_-(p_0-cq)$. Here $m-c>0$ and $0\le t_-\le1$ because $c\le1$, so $cq\le r\le p_0$ and $\int r\,dM=m-t_-(m-c)=1$. If $m=1$, set $r=p_0$. Thus $K^*$ is a probability kernel. For $h\in G$, integrate $cq\le r\le aq$ and use the density representation of L to obtain the claimed two-sided pure-DP inequalities.

For $h\in G$, clipping changes $p$ by total integral $\int|p-p_0|\,dM=\alpha+\beta$, while correction moves $p_0$ in one direction and changes its integral by $|m-1|=|\alpha-\beta|$. Thus $\int|p-r|\,dM\le\alpha+\beta+|\alpha-\beta|=2\max\{\alpha,\beta\}\le2\delta$. For probability densities with equal integral, $\sup_A|\int_A(p-r)\,dM|=\tfrac12\int|p-r|\,dM$: every event integral is bounded by the positive-part integral and $\{p\ge r\}$ attains it. Hence $\operatorname{TV}(K(h,\cdot),K^*(h,\cdot))\le\delta$ on $G$. This TV function is measurable: applying the approximation argument of step 2.1 to $K+K^*$ shows its supremum may be taken over $\mathcal C$, whose kernel evaluations are measurable. Since $G$ is conull, integration proves the asserted bound.

$$

$$

$$\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B := \sigma(\{A \times B : A \in \mathcal A,\ B \in \mathcal B\}),$$

unique probability measure $P$ on
$$ \left(\prod_{n\ge0}E_n,\ \bigotimes_{n\ge0}\mathcal E_n\right) $$ whose finite-prefix laws are the prescribed iterated integrals $$ \mu_0(dx_0)K_0(x_0,dx_1)K_1(x_0,x_1,dx_2)\cdots K_{r-1}(x_0,\ldots,x_{r-1},dx_r). $$
In particular, if every $E_n=E$ and
$K_n(x_0,\ldots,x_n,A)=K(x_n,A)$, the coordinate process is a homogeneous
$K$-chain with initial law $\mu_0$.

Assume AC. Let $(E,\mathcal E)$ and $(F,\mathcal F)$ be standard Borel spaces, let $\lambda$ be a probability measure on $E$, and let $M$ and $R$ be probability kernels from $E$ to $F$. Suppose $M(x,\cdot)\ll R(x,\cdot)$ for $\lambda$-almost every $x$. Then there is an $(\mathcal E\otimes\mathcal F)$-measurable function $r:E\times F\to[0,\infty]$ such that, for $\lambda$-almost every $x$ and every $B\in\mathcal F$,
$$M(x,B)=\int_B r(x,y)\,R(x,dy).$$
The exceptional set in $x$ is a single null set, independent of $B$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $P$ and $Q$ be probability measures on a measurable space measurably isomorphic to a Polish space, and let $\varepsilon\ge0$. If
$$
P(A)\le e^\varepsilon Q(A)\quad\text{and}\quad Q(A)\le e^\varepsilon P(A)
$$
for every measurable set $A$, then their Kullback–Leibler divergence satisfies
$$
D(P\|Q)\le\varepsilon(e^\varepsilon-1).
$$

Assume AC. Let $H$ and $Y$ be measurable spaces measurably isomorphic to Polish spaces, let $\lambda$ be a probability measure on $H$, and let $K,L$ be probability kernels from $H$ to $Y$. Let $\varepsilon\ge0$ and $0\le\delta\le1$. Suppose that for $\lambda$-almost every $h$, both inequalities
$$
K(h,A)\le e^\varepsilon L(h,A)+\delta,\qquad L(h,A)\le e^\varepsilon K(h,A)+\delta
$$
hold for every measurable $A\subseteq Y$. Then there is a probability kernel $K^*$ from $H$ to $Y$ such that for $\lambda$-almost every $h$ and every measurable $A\subseteq Y$,
$$
e^{-\varepsilon}L(h,A)\le K^*(h,A)\le e^\varepsilon L(h,A),
$$
and
$$
\int_H \operatorname{TV}(K(h,\cdot),K^*(h,\cdot))\,\lambda(dh)\le\delta,
$$
where $\operatorname{TV}(P,Q)=\sup_A|P(A)-Q(A)|$ over measurable events.

Let $(Z,\mathcal Z)$ and $(E,\mathcal E)$ be standard-Borel spaces, let $\mu$ be a probability measure on $Z$, and let $K,L:Z\rightsquigarrow E$ be supplied probability kernels. Define their **conditional KL divergence with base $\mu$** by
$$D_\mu(K\|L):=\int_Z D(K(z,\cdot)\|L(z,\cdot))\,\mu(dz)\in[0,+\infty].$$
The integrand is measurable by [[thm-conditional-kl-is-measurable]], so this is a well-defined nonnegative extended integral. No absolute-continuity assumption is imposed on individual fibers; a singular fiber has divergence $+\infty$. Changing supplied kernel versions on a $\mu$-null set does not change the integral.

Let K,L be probability kernels from a measurable space $(Z,\mathcal Z)$ into a standard-Borel space $(E,\mathcal E)$. Then $z\mapsto D(K(z,\cdot)\|L(z,\cdot))$ is $\mathcal Z$-measurable, with $+\infty$ allowed. Consequently the integral used to define conditional KL is well-defined.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ be a probability space, $\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F$ a sub-sigma-algebra, and $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ integrable. A **conditional-expectation version of $X$ given $\mathcal G$** is a real, $\mathcal G$-measurable, integrable function $Y$ such that $\int_A Y\,dP=\int_A X\,dP$ for every $A\in\mathcal G$. No completeness of $\mathcal G$ is assumed.

Expectation means the integral of [[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]]. Integrable representatives use [[def-l-one-of-a-measure]]; quotient notation is introduced after uniqueness.

Assume AC. Let $(M_k,\mathcal F_k)_{k=0}^n$ be a martingale. Suppose finite $\mathcal F_{k-1}$-measurable $A_k,B_k$ and deterministic $c_k\ge0$ satisfy
$$A_k\le M_k-M_{k-1}\le B_k,\qquad B_k-A_k\le c_k$$
almost surely. Then for every $t>0$,
$$\mathbb P(M_n-M_0\ge t)\le \exp\!\left(-\frac{2t^2}{\sum_{k=1}^n c_k^2}\right),$$
and the analogous lower-tail bound holds, with the zero-denominator expression interpreted as $0$.

Let $P$ and $Q$ be probability measures on a measurable space. Suppose $\varepsilon\ge0$, $0\le\delta\le1$, and $P(A)\le e^\varepsilon Q(A)+\delta$ for every measurable set $A$. Then every measurable function $g$ with $0\le g\le1$ satisfies

$$
\int g\,dP\le e^\varepsilon\int g\,dQ+\delta.
$$

Let $\mu$ be a sigma-finite positive measure and let $\nu$ be a signed measure or a finite complex measure with $\nu\ll\mu$. If $h$ is a representative of $d\nu/d\mu$, then
$$\nu(E)=\int_E h\,d\mu\qquad(E\in\mathcal A).$$
More generally, if
$$g=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\mathbf 1_{E_j}$$
is the canonical disjoint representation of a simple measurable function and $|\nu|(E_j)<+\infty$ for every $j$, then
$$\int g\,d\nu=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\int_{E_j} h\,d\mu.$$
In particular, whenever the Lebesgue integral of $gh$ is defined, one has
$$\int g\,d\nu=\int gh\,d\mu.$$

Let K be a finite kernel from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$, in particular a probability kernel, or a uniformly sigma-finite kernel with the specified exhaustion of the kernel definition. For every nonnegative $\Sigma\otimes\Tau$-measurable function $f:S\times T\to[0,\infty]$, the function
$$I_f(s)=\int_T f(s,t)\,K(s,dt)$$
is $\Sigma$-measurable, with infinity allowed. For a real product-measurable f, the set $D=\{s:I_{|f|}(s)<\infty\}$ is measurable, and its signed integral on D, extended by zero on $S\setminus D$, is a measurable real function. No assertion here is made for a general kernel lacking a common measurable finite-mass exhaustion.

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B)$ be measurable spaces, and let
$$f : X \times Y \to \overline{\mathbb R}$$
be $(\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B,\mathcal B(\overline{\mathbb R}))$-measurable.
Then $f_x : Y \to \overline{\mathbb R}$ is $\mathcal B$-measurable for every
$x \in X$, and $f^y : X \to \overline{\mathbb R}$ is $\mathcal A$-measurable
for every $y \in Y$.

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because [[cor-exponential-is-a-bijection-onto-positive-reals]] states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space.

- If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable, its **expectation** is the
  extended-valued integral
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P\in[0,+\infty].$$
- If $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ or $X:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ is integrable in the sense
  of [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]], its
  **expectation** is again
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P,$$
  now a finite real or complex number.

For an integrable real random variable,
$$\mathbb E[X]=\mathbb E[X^+]-\mathbb E[X^-],$$
where $X^+$ and $X^-$ are its positive and negative parts.

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.

derivations.claim: Fix neighboring databases $D,D'$. By [F2], every finite history space is standard Borel. To apply the infinite-sequence form of [F3], append after round $k$ a singleton output space and its unique probability kernel at every later round. The first $k$ coordinates of the resulting path law have exactly the desired finite transcript law; do this for $D$ and $D'$ to obtain $P$ and $Q$. Event evaluations of these laws are measurable in the database by [F1].

We first prove the one-sided estimate from $P$ to $Q$. Set $P_0^*=Q_0$ equal to the point mass on the empty history. Recursively, after constructing the modified $D$-transcript prefix law $P_{i-1}^*$, apply [F6] to the round-$i$ pair $K_i(D,h,\cdot),K_i(D',h,\cdot)$ with base history law $\lambda_i=P_{i-1}^*$. This gives a probability kernel $K_i^*$ that is pure $\varepsilon$ relative to $K_i(D',h,\cdot)$ in both event directions for $\lambda_i$-almost every $h$, with $\int\operatorname{TV}(K_i(D,h,\cdot),K_i^*(h,\cdot))P_{i-1}^*(dh)\le\delta$. Composing the finite modified sequence by [F3] gives a law $P^*$ and its prefix laws $P_i^*$.

The prefix laws $P_i^*$ and $Q_i$ are mutually absolutely continuous for each $i$. They agree at the empty history. If they are equivalent at $i-1$, then for a product-measurable event $B$ with $Q_i(B)=0$, the iterated integral formula [F3] gives $K_i(D',h,B_h)=0$ for $Q_{i-1}$-almost every $h$, hence for $P_{i-1}^*$-almost every $h$. The pure reverse inequality from step 1.2 gives $K_i^*(h,B_h)=0$, so $P_i^*(B)=0$. Reversing the two kernels proves the converse; induction gives prefix equivalence.

For each $i$, apply [F4] with base measure $P_{i-1}^*$ to obtain a jointly measurable density $r_i(h,y)$ of $K_i^*(h,\cdot)$ with respect to $K_i(D',h,\cdot)$ on one common conull history set. The pure event inequalities imply $e^{-\varepsilon}\le r_i\le e^\varepsilon$ almost surely there: if either bound failed on a positive-measure fiber set, some level set separated from that bound by $1/n$ would contradict one event inequality. Clip $r_i$ everywhere to $[e^{-\varepsilon},e^\varepsilon]$; Borel composition preserves measurability, the density is unchanged on the conull set, and $X_i(h,y)=\ln r_i(h,y)$ is jointly measurable with $|X_i|\le\varepsilon$.

We prove the density formula by induction on prefix length. At the first round, [F4] gives $dP_1^*/dQ_1=r_1$. Suppose $R_{i-1}=\prod_{j<i}r_j$ is the density on the first $i-1$ outputs. For a measurable event $A$ on the first $i$ outputs, [F3] gives $P_i^*(A)=\int P_{i-1}^*(dh)\int\mathbf1_A(h,y)K_i^*(h,dy)$. For almost every $h$, [F4] replaces the inner integral by $\int\mathbf1_A(h,y)r_i(h,y)K_i(D',h,dy)$. Applying [F11] to the outer prefix integral with density $R_{i-1}$ yields $P_i^*(A)=\int Q_{i-1}(dh)R_{i-1}(h)\int\mathbf1_A(h,y)r_i(h,y)K_i(D',h,dy)=\int_A R_{i-1}(h)r_i(h,y)Q_i(dh,dy)$. This proves the induction and hence $dP^*/dQ=R=\prod_{i=1}^k r_i(H_{i-1},Y_i)$. Since every factor is positive and bounded, [F15] gives $\ln R=\sum_{i=1}^kX_i(H_{i-1},Y_i)$ almost surely under both laws.

Put $m_i(h)=\int X_i(h,y)K_i^*(h,dy)$. By the density formula and KL definition, $m_i(h)=D(K_i^*(h,\cdot)\|K_i(D',h,\cdot))\le b$ for $P_{i-1}^*$-almost every $h$, using [F5]. It is measurable by [F7] and [F12]. For every measurable prefix event $C$, the iterated-prefix identity [F3] gives $\int_{\{H_{i-1}\in C\}}X_i\,dP^*=\int_Cm_i(h)P_{i-1}^*(dh)$. Thus [F8] identifies $m_i(H_{i-1})$ as the conditional expectation of $X_i$ given the previous transcript. By [F14], the variables are integrable, so $M_j=\sum_{i\le j}(X_i-m_i(H_{i-1}))$ is a martingale. Each increment lies in the history-measurable interval $[-\varepsilon-m_i,\varepsilon-m_i]$, of length $2\varepsilon$.

If $\varepsilon=0$, every $X_i=0$, so $P^*=Q$ and the pure transcript has zero privacy loss. If $\varepsilon>0$, apply [F9] to step 4.2 with $c_i=2\varepsilon$ and $t=\varepsilon\sqrt{2k\ln(1/\delta')}$. It gives $P^*(M_k\ge t)\le\delta'$. Since $\sum_i m_i\le kb$ almost surely, the privacy loss exceeds $\varepsilon'=kb+t$ with probability at most $\delta'$. For any event $A$, split it into $A\cap\{\ln R\le\varepsilon'\}$ and $A\cap\{\ln R>\varepsilon'\}$; the density formula in step 4.1 bounds the first probability by $e^{\varepsilon'}Q(A)$ and the second by $\delta'$. Thus $P^*(A)\le e^{\varepsilon'}Q(A)+\delta'$. Applying the same argument under $Q$ with the roles reversed gives $Q(A)\le e^{\varepsilon'}P^*(A)+\delta'$, because the conditional kernels are pure in both directions and [F5] bounds both KL orientations.

We compare $P$ and $P^*$ in total variation. For $i=0,\ldots,k$, let $H_i$ be the transcript law that uses the modified $D$ kernels for rounds $1,\ldots,i$ and the original $D$ kernels for rounds $i+1,\ldots,k$. Consecutive laws share the modified prefix through round $i-1$, whose law is $P_{i-1}^*$, and differ only in the round-$i$ kernel; after that round they use the same continuation kernels. For any final event, integrating that common continuation gives a measurable conditional probability $g(h,y)$ in $[0,1]$ by [F12]. The two-sided test-function bound [F10] and the integrated TV bound in step 1.2 yield $\operatorname{TV}(H_{i-1},H_i)\le\delta$. The triangle inequality gives $\operatorname{TV}(P,P^*)\le k\delta$, hence $P(A)\le P^*(A)+k\delta$. Combining with step 5.1 proves $P(A)\le e^{\varepsilon'}Q(A)+k\delta+\delta'$.

Repeat steps 1.2–6.1 with $D'$ as the modified side and $D$ as the reference side. This gives $Q(A)\le e^{\varepsilon'}P(A)+k\delta+\delta'$. The ordered pair and event were arbitrary, so [F1] proves the stated differential-privacy guarantee. The condition $k\delta+\delta'\le1$ keeps the additive parameter in its declared nontrivial range; no step weakens the claimed epsilon.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $U$ be a nonempty set of possible records and let $\mathbb N_0=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$. A database is a function $D:U\to\mathbb N_0$ with finite support $\operatorname{supp}(D)=\{u\in U:D(u)\ne0\}$; $D(u)$ is the number of occurrences of record $u$. Let $\mathcal D$ be the set of databases and equip it with the power-set sigma-algebra. For $u\in U$, let $\mathbf 1_{\{u\}}$ be the function that is one at $u$ and zero elsewhere. Two databases $D,D'\in\mathcal D$ are neighbors, written $D\sim D'$, when $D'=D+\mathbf 1_{\{u\}}$ or $D=D'+\mathbf 1_{\{u\}}$ for some $u\in U$.

A randomized mechanism with output measurable space $(Y,\mathcal B)$ is a probability kernel $K$ from $\mathcal D$ to $Y$: for each $D\in\mathcal D$, $A\mapsto K(D,A)$ is a probability measure on $(Y,\mathcal B)$, and for each $A\in\mathcal B$, $D\mapsto K(D,A)$ is measurable. Given $\varepsilon\ge0$ and $0\le\delta\le1$, the mechanism is $(\varepsilon,\delta)$-differentially private if, for every ordered neighboring pair $D\sim D'$ and every output event $A\in\mathcal B$,

$$
K(D,A)\le e^{\varepsilon}K(D',A)+\delta.
$$

The mechanism is $\varepsilon$-differentially private, or pure $\varepsilon$-differentially private, when $\delta=0$. The ordered-pair quantifier includes both directions because $\sim$ is symmetric.

Let $d\ge1$ and let $f:\mathcal D\to\mathbb R^d$ be a query on databases with the add/remove adjacency relation. Write $\|x\|_1=\sum_{j=1}^d|x_j|$. When the set of adjacent-pair differences has an attained finite maximum, the global $L^1$ sensitivity of $f$ is

$$
\Delta_1 f=\max_{D\sim D'}\|f(D)-f(D')\|_1.
$$

The sensitivity is finite when this maximum is finite.

Let $\mathcal D$ be the finite-support count functions on a nonempty record universe, with neighbors formed by adding or removing one record occurrence. Input a database $D\in\mathcal D$, a finite-dimensional query $f:\mathcal D\to\mathbb R^d$ with finite global $L^1$ sensitivity $\Delta_1 f$, and a parameter $\varepsilon>0$. If $\Delta_1 f>0$, draw $Z$ from the finite product law $\operatorname{Lap}(\Delta_1 f/\varepsilon)^{\otimes d}$ and release $f(D)+Z$. If $\Delta_1 f=0$, release $f(D)$ deterministically. The output space is $\mathbb R^d$ with its Borel sigma-algebra. Equivalently, for each Borel event $A$, the output kernel is $K(D,A)=\int\mathbf1_A(f(D)+z)\operatorname{Lap}(\Delta_1f/\varepsilon)^{\otimes d}(dz)$ when $\Delta_1f>0$, and $K(D,A)=\mathbf1_A(f(D))$ when $\Delta_1f=0$.

For every finite-dimensional query $f:\mathcal D\to\mathbb R^d$ with $d\ge1$ and finite global $L^1$ sensitivity, and every $\varepsilon>0$, the Laplace mechanism is $(\varepsilon,0)$-differentially private under add/remove adjacency.

derivations.claim: If $D'$ is obtained from $D$ by adding one occurrence of $u$, then $f(D')-f(D)=P(u)\in\{0,1\}$; removing one occurrence gives the negative of this change. Thus every adjacent difference has absolute value at most $1$. The empty database and the database containing only $u_0$ are neighbors and their counts differ by $1$, so the maximum is attained and $\Delta_1f=1$.

By [F3], the scalar release uses scale $\Delta_1f/\varepsilon=1/\varepsilon$ and is exactly the stated noisy count. This query has finite dimension one and sensitivity one, so [F4] proves its $(\varepsilon,0)$ guarantee.

Let $\mathcal D$ be the finite-support count functions on a nonempty record universe, with add/remove-one-occurrence adjacency. Let $R$ be a nonempty finite set independent of the database, and let $u:\mathcal D\times R\to\mathbb R$ be a real-valued utility. When the set of adjacent-pair utility differences has an attained finite maximum, the global utility sensitivity of $u$ is
$$
\Delta_u=\max_{D\sim D',\,r\in R}|u(D,r)-u(D',r)|.
$$
The sensitivity is positive when $\Delta_u>0$; the exponential mechanism on this page uses that positive-sensitivity case.

Let $\mathcal D$ be the finite-support count functions on a nonempty record universe, with add/remove-one-occurrence adjacency. Input a database $D\in\mathcal D$, a parameter $\varepsilon>0$, a nonempty finite database-independent range $R$, and a real-valued utility $u:\mathcal D\times R\to\mathbb R$ with finite positive global utility sensitivity $\Delta_u$. For each $r\in R$, set
$$ w_D(r)=\exp\!\left(\frac{\varepsilon u(D,r)}{2\Delta_u}\right),\qquad Z_D=\sum_{s\in R}w_D(s). $$
Output $r\in R$ with probability $w_D(r)/Z_D$. Equip $R$ with its power-set sigma-algebra and define $K(D,B)=\sum_{r\in B}w_D(r)/Z_D$ for each $B\subseteq R$; this is the probability kernel from databases to outputs.

Let $\mathcal D$ be the set of finite-support record-count databases, with neighbors defined by adding or removing one record occurrence. Let $R$ be a nonempty finite set independent of the database, and let $u:\mathcal D\times R\to\mathbb R$ be a real-valued utility with finite positive attained global utility sensitivity $\Delta_u$. For $\varepsilon>0$, use weights $w_D(r)=\exp(\varepsilon u(D,r)/(2\Delta_u))$ and normalize them over $R$ as in the exponential mechanism. Its output law is $(\varepsilon,0)$-differentially private. For a fixed database $D$, let
$$ \operatorname{OPT}_u(D)=\max_{r\in R}u(D,r),\qquad R_{\operatorname{OPT}}=\{r\in R:u(D,r)=\operatorname{OPT}_u(D)\}. $$
For every $t>0$, if $M(D)$ denotes the random output, then
$$
\Pr\!\left[u(D,M(D))\le\operatorname{OPT}_u(D)-\frac{2\Delta_u}{\varepsilon}\left(\ln\frac{|R|}{|R_{\operatorname{OPT}}|}+t\right)\right]\le e^{-t}.
$$

derivations.claim: For the first utility, every score is independent of $D$, so every adjacent-pair difference is zero and $\Delta_u=0$ by [F2]. This fails the positive-sensitivity hypothesis in [F3], so the algorithm is not defined for that utility.

For the second utility, adding or removing a record other than $u_*$ leaves $s(D)$ unchanged; adding or removing $u_*$ changes it by at most one. The empty database and the database with one occurrence of $u_*$ are neighbors and change $s$ from zero to one. The score at $a$ is constant, and the score at $b$ changes by exactly the change in $s$, so the maximum adjacent score difference is attained and equals $\Delta_u=1$.

With $\Delta_u=1$, the weights are $w_D(a)=e^{\varepsilon/2}$ and $w_D(b)=e^{\varepsilon(1-s(D))/2}$. Normalizing their sum gives the displayed selection probability. Since the range is finite nonempty and the sensitivity is positive, [F4] proves the privacy claim.

No countable-generation hypothesis enters this construction.

Set $T_0=P_0=Q_0$. Given $T_{i-1}$, form $R_i=T_{i-1}\otimes K_i$ and $S_i=T_{i-1}\otimes L_i$. Apply [F3] with history law $T_{i-1}$ to obtain a probability $T_i$ on $H_i$ with marginal $T_{i-1}$, $S_i/a\le T_i\le aS_i$, and $\operatorname{TV}(R_i,T_i)\le\delta$, where $a=\exp(\varepsilon)\ge1$ by [F9]. The hypotheses hold at every history, hence also under the modified history law. These are measures only; no conditional kernel for $T_i$ is required. Finite iteration yields consistent prefix marginals of the final probability $T_k$. Moreover [F5], applied to $h\mapsto K_i(h,B_h)\in[0,1]$, gives $\operatorname{TV}(P_i,R_i)\le\operatorname{TV}(P_{i-1},T_{i-1})$. Thus the triangle inequality and induction give $\operatorname{TV}(P_i,T_i)\le i\delta$.

By [A1] choose a product-measurable density $r_i=dT_i/dS_i$. The measure bounds in step 2.1 force $a^{-1}\le r_i\le a$ almost everywhere, since otherwise a level set separated from one bound contradicts that bound after integration. Clip the representative into this positive interval everywhere. Write $Z_i=\prod_{j\le i}r_j$ as a function on $H_i$, with $Z_0=1$. We prove $dT_i/dQ_i=Z_i$ by induction. If $dT_{i-1}/dQ_{i-1}=Z_{i-1}$, then for any nonnegative measurable $g$ on $H_i$, [F2] and [F4] give $\int g\,dT_i=\int gr_i\,dS_i=\int T_{i-1}(dh)\int g(h,y)r_i(h,y)L_i(h,dy)=\int Q_{i-1}(dh)Z_{i-1}(h)\int g(h,y)r_i(h,y)L_i(h,dy)=\int gZ_{i-1}r_i\,dQ_i$. The base is the common point mass. Hence $Z_i$ is the asserted density and is everywhere positive and finite. In particular $\log Z_k=\sum_i X_i$ for the measurable prefix variables $X_i=\log r_i$, each in $[-\varepsilon,\varepsilon]$.

Define measurable functions on $H_{i-1}$ by $u_i(h)=\int r_i(h,y)L_i(h,dy)$ and $m_i(h)=\int r_i(h,y)\log r_i(h,y)L_i(h,dy)$. They are finite by the bounds in step 3.1. Because $T_i$ and $S_i$ have the same history marginal $T_{i-1}$, their density identity on $C\times Y_i$ gives $\int_Cu_i\,dT_{i-1}=T_{i-1}(C)$ for every $C$, so $u_i=1$ almost everywhere under $T_{i-1}$. On this conull set, $\log r_i\le r_i-1$ gives $\int\log r_i\,dL_i\le0$. Therefore $m_i\le\int(r_i-1)\log r_i\,dL_i\le\varepsilon\int|r_i-1|\,dL_i$. For every $a^{-1}\le r\le a$, $|r-1|\le(a-1)\min\{r,1\}$, by separately checking $r\ge1$ and $r\le1$. Thus $m_i\le\varepsilon(a-1)=:b$ almost everywhere. This scalar conditional calculation supplies the entropy bound without a fiberwise RN identity.

Work on $(H_k,T_k)$ with the filtration $\mathcal F_i$ generated by the first $i$ coordinates. For any measurable history event $C$, consistency of marginals, the density identity for $T_i$ relative to $S_i$, and the iterated-integral formula give $\int_{\{H_{i-1}\in C\}}X_i\,dT_k=\int_Cm_i(h)T_{i-1}(dh)$. Hence $m_i(H_{i-1})$ is a version of $\mathbb E_{T_k}[X_i\mid\mathcal F_{i-1}]$ by [F6]. It is bounded, as are the $X_i$, so $M_j=\sum_{i\le j}(X_i-m_i(H_{i-1}))$ is an integrable martingale. Its $i$th increment lies in the $\mathcal F_{i-1}$-measurable interval $[-\varepsilon-m_i,\varepsilon-m_i]$, whose length is $2\varepsilon$.

If $\varepsilon=0$, all $r_i=1$, so $T_k=Q_k$ and the desired one-sided bound follows from step 2.1 with error $k\delta$. If $\varepsilon>0$, put $t=\varepsilon\sqrt{2k\ln(1/\delta')}>0$. Applying [F7] with interval lengths $2\varepsilon$ gives $T_k(M_k\ge t)\le\exp(-t^2/(2k\varepsilon^2))=\delta'$. Step 4.1 bounds $\sum_i m_i\le kb$, so $T_k(\log Z_k>kb+t)\le\delta'$. Set $\varepsilon'=kb+t$. For every transcript event $B$, split at $\log Z_k\le\varepsilon'$ and use the density from step 3.1 to obtain $T_k(B)\le e^{\varepsilon'}Q_k(B)+\delta'$. Then step 2.1 gives $P_k(B)\le e^{\varepsilon'}Q_k(B)+k\delta+\delta'$.

The preceding construction applies to every ordered neighboring pair. In particular repeat it with $D,D'$ interchanged, constructing a new modified measure on that side, to get $Q_k(B)\le e^{\varepsilon'}P_k(B)+k\delta+\delta'$. This proves differential privacy by [F1]. The proof includes $k=1$, $\delta=0$, and equality $k\delta+\delta'=1$; $0<\delta'<1$ makes the logarithm finite and positive. All database event evaluations are measurable by the power-set database convention in [F1]. No modified law, density, or exceptional set needs to be selected measurably in the database pair: the event inequality has been proved for each pair separately.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $U$ be a nonempty set of possible records and let $\mathbb N_0=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$. A database is a function $D:U\to\mathbb N_0$ with finite support $\operatorname{supp}(D)=\{u\in U:D(u)\ne0\}$; $D(u)$ is the number of occurrences of record $u$. Let $\mathcal D$ be the set of databases and equip it with the power-set sigma-algebra. For $u\in U$, let $\mathbf 1_{\{u\}}$ be the function that is one at $u$ and zero elsewhere. Two databases $D,D'\in\mathcal D$ are neighbors, written $D\sim D'$, when $D'=D+\mathbf 1_{\{u\}}$ or $D=D'+\mathbf 1_{\{u\}}$ for some $u\in U$.

A randomized mechanism with output measurable space $(Y,\mathcal B)$ is a probability kernel $K$ from $\mathcal D$ to $Y$: for each $D\in\mathcal D$, $A\mapsto K(D,A)$ is a probability measure on $(Y,\mathcal B)$, and for each $A\in\mathcal B$, $D\mapsto K(D,A)$ is measurable. Given $\varepsilon\ge0$ and $0\le\delta\le1$, the mechanism is $(\varepsilon,\delta)$-differentially private if, for every ordered neighboring pair $D\sim D'$ and every output event $A\in\mathcal B$,

$$
K(D,A)\le e^{\varepsilon}K(D',A)+\delta.
$$

The mechanism is $\varepsilon$-differentially private, or pure $\varepsilon$-differentially private, when $\delta=0$. The ordered-pair quantifier includes both directions because $\sim$ is symmetric.

Let $\mathcal D$ be the finite-support count functions on a nonempty record universe, with neighbors formed by adding or removing one record occurrence. Let $k\ge1$ and let $\mathcal Y_1,\ldots,\mathcal Y_k$ be measurable output spaces. For each round $i$, let $K_i(D,h,\cdot)$ be a probability kernel on $\mathcal Y_i$ for every database $D\in\mathcal D$ and prior transcript $h\in\mathcal Y_1\times\cdots\times\mathcal Y_{i-1}$. Suppose that for every neighboring pair $D\sim D'$, every prior transcript $h$, and every measurable event $A\subseteq\mathcal Y_i$,
$$
K_i(D,h,A)\le e^{\varepsilon_i}K_i(D',h,A)+\delta_i,
$$
where $\varepsilon_i\ge0$ and $\delta_i\ge0$. If $\sum_{i=1}^k\delta_i\le1$, then the full transcript is $(\sum_{i=1}^k\varepsilon_i,\sum_{i=1}^k\delta_i)$-differentially private on the finite product sigma-algebra.

Assume AC. Let $\mathcal D$ be a set equipped with its power-set sigma-algebra and a symmetric adjacency relation $\sim$; this includes finite-support record-count databases with neighbors differing by one added or removed occurrence. Let $k\ge1$, let $Y_1,\ldots,Y_k$ be arbitrary measurable output spaces, and let round $i$ be a probability kernel $K_i(D,h,\cdot)$ on $Y_i$, measurable in the previous transcript $h\in H_{i-1}=\prod_{j<i}Y_j$ for each database $D$. Suppose that for every ordered neighboring pair $D\sim D'$, every $i$, every $h$, and every measurable $A\subseteq Y_i$,
$$K_i(D,h,A)\le e^\varepsilon K_i(D',h,A)+\delta,$$
where $\varepsilon\ge0$ and $0\le\delta\le1$. If $0<\delta'<1$ and $k\delta+\delta'\le1$, then the full transcript, on the finite product sigma-algebra, is $(\varepsilon',k\delta+\delta')$-differentially private, where
$$\varepsilon'=\varepsilon\sqrt{2k\ln(1/\delta')}+k\varepsilon(e^\varepsilon-1).$$
